questions.question: Explain how a wedge gives a mechanical advantage, using an axe as your example, and state why a thinner wedge gives a greater advantage.
questions.expected_answer: A wedge is an inclined plane driven into a material. When an axe is swung into a log the thin edge enters and the widening sides push the two halves apart, converting the downward force of the swing into a much larger sideways splitting force. A thinner wedge moves the sides apart by a smaller distance for each unit of forward movement, so by the force-distance trade the sideways force is larger; mechanical advantage is roughly the wedge's length divided by its thickness.

questions.question: Describe a wheel and axle, explain where its mechanical advantage comes from, and give one example used for force and one used for speed.
questions.expected_answer: A wheel and axle is a large wheel fixed to a smaller axle so they turn together. A point on the rim travels much further in one turn than a point on the axle, so a small force on the rim becomes a large force at the axle; the mechanical advantage is wheel radius divided by axle radius, like a lever turning about its centre. For force: a tap handle, steering wheel or screwdriver. For speed: a bicycle wheel driven at the axle so the rim moves fast, with a mechanical advantage below 1.

questions.question: Give two jobs for which a designer would choose a wedge and two for which a designer would choose a wheel and axle, with an example of each, and say how each might be used in the PAT structure.
questions.expected_answer: Wedge: splitting (axe), cutting (knife or chisel), holding (door wedge, tapered peg), slight lifting (wedge under a cupboard). Wheel and axle: turning with more force (tap, winch handle), turning faster (bicycle wheel), reducing friction (trolley or wheelbarrow wheels). In the PAT, a wedge-shaped foot can hold the structure steady on an uneven surface, and a wheel and axle turned by a crank can drive the moving mechanism.
